title: Dietary Control of the Pro-Metastatic Niche in Colorectal Cancer
text:
Colorectal cancer is one of the major causes of all cancer related deaths and a critical challenge in colorectal
cancer outcome is lack of therapies designed to combat metastatic disease. Diet and obesity are among the
major lifestyle choices that can affect colorectal cancer risk, however not much is known about how pro-obesity
diets can affect cancer metastasis. This proposal investigates the molecular mechanisms underlying how pro-
obesity high fat diets impact colorectal cancer metastasis, revealing therapeutic vulnerabilities and enabling
evidence-based effective dietary recommendations.

title: Lysosomal control of plasma membrane -endoplasmic reticulum membrane contacts regulates neuronal excitability
text:
Alterations in the distribution of cellular cholesterol in the brain has been linked to a host of chronic
neurodegenerative disorders. This study will investigate the mechanisms through which lysosomal cholesterol
transport can modify the distribution and activity of ion channels to shape neuronal function. The results from the
proposed work could inform novel therapeutic strategies to treat neuropathophysiological disorders.

title: Unraveling myeloid-mediated mechanisms of immunotherapy resistance in prostate cancer bone metastases at single-cell resolution
text:
Prostate cancer is the most common male malignancy, with bone being the predominant site (>70%) of
metastases in patients with advanced prostate cancer. Patients with bone metastases tend to have poorer
responses to immunotherapy compared to those without bone involvement, suggesting the presence of an
immunosuppressive niche within bone. To discover molecular targets for improving immunotherapeutic
strategies, we will focus on identifying the specific cells and corresponding signals that contribute to
immunotherapy resistance in the tumor microenvironment.

title: Cross-Species Multidisciplinary Training in Alcohol Research
text: There is a shortage of researchers with the high levels of interdisciplinary skills needed to make progress in understanding the etiology and improving clinical treatment of alcohol use disorder (AUD), a major public health problem. The objective of this training grant is to educate the next generation of researchers focused on i) elucidating the risk factors for and outcomes of problem alcohol use, ii) understanding the behavioral and molecular causes and consequences of problematic alcohol use, and iii) contributing to the translation of these basic findings into improvements in both treatment and prevention of AUD. The training in this program aims to educate an interdisciplinary work force of researchers with a solid knowledge of multiple relevant areas, including genetics, behavior, neurobiology, data science and clinical treatment who will be prepared to have an impact on the health of millions of individuals affected by AUD.

title: Racial Disparities in Parkinson Disease- Clinical Phenotype, Management and Genetics
text:
Parkinson disease (PD) is a progressive, disabling neurological disorder, but the impact
of the disease on Black patients with PD is unclear due to less research in this
population. This study investigates racial disparities by studying symptoms and signs,
management, and genotype relationships in Black PD participants in comparison to a
group of White PD participants. This study will result in new scientific knowledge
regarding PD in the Black population by characterizing the basis for racial disparities,
raising awareness of differences in PD recognition and management, and educating
patients in this underserved and understudied population.

title: Mechanisms of Macrophage Manipulation by pathogenic SFG Rickettsia: Role of Mitochondrial and Immune Pathways
text:
PROJECT NARRATIVE.
The incidence of spotted fever group (SFG) rickettsioses (SFR) is rising worldwide, with the expanding
geographic distribution of SFG rickettsiae posing a significant public health threat. With our work, we seek to
gain a more comprehensive understanding of the complex SFG Rickettsia-macrophage interactions and
to fill fundamental gaps in knowledge of immune evasion mechanisms and pathogenicity in rickettsiae.
Our studies will reveal new mechanisms that can be leveraged to develop new approaches to treating rickettsial
infections via modulation of mitochondrial homeostasis and enhanced immune responses against rickettsial
infections.

title: Real-time modeling and perturbation of stimulus-shaped neural manifolds
text:
The goal of this project is to develop new real-time methods for constructing neural manifolds shaped by external
stimuli and designing perturbations of neural dynamics with direct and indirect stimulations. Our approach will
enable new classes of experiments to causally test hypotheses of how population dynamics contribute to neural
circuit function. With these methods, we will obtain new insight into the neurobiological mechanisms underlying
the encoding and processing of complex external stimuli.

title: Immune Activation and Region-specific Myocardial Arrhythmic Substrate in Sudden Cardiac Death Victims with HIV
text:
We discovered that people with HIV (PWH) have higher rates of autopsy-confirmed sudden cardiac death (SCD)
and higher levels of interstitial myocardial fibrosis (microscopic scarring of the heart) which may underlie lethal
heart rhythms. Leveraging our unique biobank of autopsy tissue from victims of SCD, we will test the hypothesis
that immune cell activation in the hearts of PWH, with particular specificity for the outermost layer of the heart,
increases the risk of lethal arrhythmias and SCD via increased tissue fibrosis and disruption of cardiac electrical
conduction.

title: A Single Shot Measles Vectored Rabies Vaccine for Children
text:
Rabies is a neglected zoonotic disease, with a global estimated cost of US$ 8.6 billion per year, predominantly
affecting children in remote rural locations. The ineffectiveness of the current dog rabies prevention efforts and
the lack of a cost-effective childhood pre-exposure rabies vaccine leave children vulnerable to this deadly
disease. This grant application proposes to develop a single shot measles vectored rabies vaccine for children
that could offer a feasible and affordable solution for effectively combating this vaccine-preventable disease.

title: Early-Stage Technology Development to Enable Rigorous and Reproducible Fungal Metatranscriptomics in Human Vaginal Samples
text:
Vaginal yeast infections afflict three out of four women and are a chronic condition for 1 out of 10; yet both
diagnostics and treatments remain insufficient, resulting in frequent misdiagnoses and disease recurrence.
Here, we will develop FRAMES, a new low-cost technology to enrich and preserve fungal RNA and enable
simultaneous measurements of fungal and human RNA interactions from the same vaginal swab. By
identifying the gene-expression signatures that distinguish harmless yeast colonization from disease, this
project will guide development of accurate diagnostics and durable therapies that break the cycle of recurrent
vaginal yeast infections, improving the health and quality of life for tens of millions of women.

title: Acoustic platform for separation, isolation, and enrichment in biomedical research
text:
Efficient separation, isolation, and enrichment of specific molecules and cells are critical research steps in biol-
ogy, biotechnology, and medicine, with each playing an important role in advancing biomedical research. Micro-
fluidic devices offer promising solutions that can achieve these steps with precise control, but these technologies
are currently limited to small amounts of sample, restricting the amount or rate of processing. In the proposed
project, these obstacles are overcome by a new technology platform, based on highly configurable arrays of
microfabricated features, that uses sound to move and trap small particles and cells for a wide variety of research
applications involving enrichment, isolation, and separation.

title: Genetic basis for persistence of Borrelia burgdorferi
text:
A portion of Lyme disease patients continue to experience persistent symptoms even after antibiotic
treatment, resulting in a condition called post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome. The cause of this
syndrome is unknown but has been proposed to be caused by continuous presence of Borrelia
burgdorferi, the causative Lyme disease agent. The experiments in this proposal will examine the
roles of the immune response and genetics play in the development of this persistent disease and
use novel state of the art tests for detection of Borrelia burgdorferi in patients with post-treatment
Lyme disease syndrome.

title: Human Pluripotent Stem Cells and Organoids for Salivary Gland Regeneration
text:
Cancer patients receiving radiation treatment for head and neck cancer or patients suffering from autoimmune
disorders such as Sjögren's syndrome suffer from salivary gland dysfunction that causes debilitating oral health
problems such as tooth decay, difficulties in chewing and speaking, and microbial infections. The proposed
research will investigate a novel strategy to derive salivary gland progenitor cells and mature organoids from
human pluripotent stem cells. The proposed work will facilitate understanding of salivary gland biology and
enable development of drug screening platforms as well as cell therapies for SG regeneration to treat
hyposalivation disorders.

title: Research Support Core (RSC)
text:
The Resource Support Core (RSC) will develop measures of biological aging that allow us to examine how sex 
differences in aging health outcomes arise. These measures will focus on physiological dysregulation and 
molecular and cellular changes which may be in response to social, environmental and hormonal conditions.

title: 3D highly-multiplexed imaging and machine learning for immunoprofiling of human and murine tumors
text:
New and emerging microscopy methods, including highly multiplexed imaging (profiling) of tissues and tumors,
promises to transform our understanding of the cancer ecosystem at a single-cell level. However, the
development and use of these methods requires a very high level expertise, which Dr. Clarence Yapp
exemplifies in his role as Director of Microscopy and Computer Vision for the Laboratory of Systems
Pharmacology (LSP) at Harvard Medical School (HMS). As an NCI Research Specialist, Yapp will continue to
support experiments in dozens of LSP-affiliated cancer research labs, develop novel 3D approaches to tissue
imaging, and provide his expertise to multiple NCI programs and consortia.

title: Developing Genetically Encoded Intrabodies to Define Retrotransposon Function in Synaptic Development
text:
This project addresses the role of mobile genetic elements, often called 'junk DNA,' in public
health, particularly in age-related neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's. We are
developing a transformative new technology to precisely target and turn off specific activities of
these genetic elements, allowing us to understand for the first time exactly how they contribute to
the decline of brain function. This foundational research is critical for identifying new therapeutic
strategies to combat neurodegeneration and promote healthy aging.

title: Human Neuromuscular Aging-on-a-Chip: Modeling Molecular and Functional Hallmarks of Skeletal Muscle Decline
text:
This project will develop a human 3D neuromuscular microphysiological system to model how aging impairs
muscle stem cell function, neuromuscular junctions, and contractile strength. The platform will enable discovery
of geroprotective drugs and personalized interventions to preserve mobility and extend healthy lifespan in older
adults. By providing a physiologically relevant human model, this work will bridge the gap between basic aging
research and clinical translation.

title: Yale Alzheimer Disease Research Center
text:
OVERALL YALE ADRC
The Yale Alzheimer Disease Research Center seeks to advance our understanding of Alzheimer’s disease with the eventual goal of translating laboratory discoveries into novel effective clinical therapies. Seven Cores (Administrative, Clinical, Data, Biomarker, Neuropathology, iPSC and Outreach) and a Research Education Component will work together to achieve this goal. Our unifying theme is a focus on the cell biology of specific neural cells, and its heterogenous disruption in Alzheimer’s disease.

title: Assay Development and High Throughput Screening (ADHTS) Core
text: Assay Development and High Throughput Screening Core (ADHTS) The goal of the Assay Development and High Throughput Screening (ADHTS) Core of the Indiana University School of Medicine Purdue University TaRget Enablement to Accelerate Therapy Development for Alzheimer's Disease (IUSM-Purdue TREAT-AD) Center is to integrate sophisticated disease biology and drug discovery capabilities and create Target Enabling Packages for the study of emerging Alzheimer's disease (AD) hypotheses (beyond amyloid beta). Accomplishing this goal will create the foundation for new classes of therapeutics to treat Alzheimer's disease. The supportive mission of the ADHTS Core is to advance target validation and enable novel drug discovery opportunities for IUSM-Purdue TREAT-AD Center targets. In collaboration with the other technical cores, we will use an integrated target assessment approach to improve target validation and facilitate the selection of targets for enablement. This work supports the design and development of individual assays and assembly into a connected set of in vitro and in vivo assays capable of providing reliable data to support novel drug discovery. In addition, the ADHTS core will develop translational biomarker strategies that support dose setting in early clinical development, thereby decreasing drug discovery risk and providing a clear path to early clinical testing. Finally, the core will disseminate essential resources such as novel reagents, assay methodologies, and data. All resources will be made available to the Alzheimer's Disease research community through the Target Enabling Packages that are posted on the AD Knowledge Portal and through direct requests made to the Center for transfer of materials. The ADHTS core directly contributes to the success of the IUSM-Purdue TREAT-AD Center through delivery of target enablement packages for the next generation of biological targets. The connected scheme of biochemical, cellular, and in vivo assays will be capable of prosecuting robust Structure Activity Relationship studies with the intention of identifying clinical candidates coupled with enabling biomarker assays positioned for translation to early clinical testing.

title: Population Science and Cancer Control Program
text: The Population Science and Cancer Control (PS) Program generates research discoveries addressing the cancer burden in the Simmons Comprehensive Cancer Center (SCCC) catchment area in North Texas and beyond. Specific aims are to: (1) Identify and evaluate predictive markers for cancer risk, early detection, progression, and treatment response, (2) Identify multi-level factors associated with cancer prevention, early detection, care delivery, and outcomes, including survivorship, and (3) Develop and test interventions to improve evidence-based cancer prevention and control, with a focus on underserved populations and safety- net healthcare systems. Informed by the SCCC Strategic Plan, PS conducts research across the cancer continuum and with an emphasis in liver, lung, breast, and kidney cancer, and the scientific themes of precision intervention for cancer prevention and control and metabolic dysregulation and obesity, Since 2020, PS has grown from 27 to 32 members who hold primary appointments in eight departments in UTSW Medical School and three departments in the Peter O’Donnell Jr. School of Public Health. Guided by the 2020 review and SCCC Strategic Plan, PS added five experts in obesity-related research and four epidemiologists. New members are Assistant (7), Associate (1), and Full Professors (4), with research foci addressing all three program aims. PS funding is on an upward trend, with $6.5M in total cancer focused funding of which $6.1M (94%) is peer-reviewed and $3.4M (52%) is from NCI, representing a 10% increase in total funding since 2020. PS generates cancer discoveries from large cohorts; study enrollment since 2020 exceeds 95K individuals, of whom most are underserved. A significant amount of PS research is conducted at Parkland Health (PH) – one of the country’s largest integrated safety-net systems serving >1M un- and under-insured patients. Via our NCI-funded PROSPR awards, PS members developed sophisticated EHR data collection/curation methods to study multi-level factors associated with completion of cancer screening processes for thousands of underserved patients. These procedures have now been translated to address research priorities in our catchment area such as early-onset colorectal cancer (CRC) and liver cancer. PS hypothesis-driven research, often through large pragmatic trials, supported strategies like the "FIT (fecal immunochemical test)-first" approach for CRC screening and identified quality improvements such as effectiveness of mailed outreach and patient navigation to facilitate liver cancer screening, particularly among underserved patients. This work influenced national guidelines for liver cancer prevention, diagnosis, and treatment and was the basis for a Liver SPORE application to NCI in 2024 (merit score 18; March 2025). During the current grant cycle, PS members authored 775 peer-reviewed publications (vs 498 in the previous cycle); 24% of these were intra-programmatic, 39%, inter-programmatic, 51%, inter-institutional publications, and 31% were in journals with an impact factor ≥10.
